content: The calorie is a unit of energy that predates the International System of Units (SI) and is primarily associated with heat. While its use has become outdated in most scientific and technical fields, replaced by the SI unit of energy, the joule (J), the calorie remains widely used in the context of food energy. The term calorie was first introduced by Professor Nicolas Clément in 1824, specifically as a kilogram-calorie, and this definition was incorporated into French and English dictionaries between 1841 and 1867. The word calorie is derived from the French term of the same spelling, which originates from the Latin word calor, meaning heat. Historically, the calorie has been defined in two primary ways, which differ by a factor of 1000: 1. Small calorie (cal): Also known as the gram calorie, this is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one gram of water by 1°C. 2. Large calorie (kcal or Calorie): Also referred to as the kilogram calorie or kilocalorie, this is the amount of energy needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of water by 1°C. It is equivalent to 1000 small calories or approximately 4.184 kilojoules (kJ). This is the definition most commonly used to describe food energy. While the term calorie is often used colloquially, the symbol kcal is sometimes employed in more formal contexts. In addition to these two main definitions, there are minor variations in the definition of the calorie, which depend on the specific experimental conditions, such as the starting temperature of the water. These variations have led to different conversion factors between calories and joules, which are numerically related to the specific heat capacity of water in SI units. As a result, several definitions of the calorie have been established over time: 1. Thermochemical calorie (calth): Defined as exactly 4.184 joules (J). 2. 15°C calorie (cal15): The energy required to heat 1 gram of air-free water from 14.5°C to 15.325 kPa (1 atmosphere). Experimental values for this calorie ranged from 4.1852 J to 4.1858 J.1855 J, with an uncertainty of ±0.0005 J. 3. 20°C calorie: The energy required to heat 1 gram of air-free water from 19.5°C to 20.325 kPa. This is approximately 4.182 J. 4. 4°C calorie: The energy required to heat 1 gram of air-free water from 3.5°C to 4.325 kPa. 5. Mean calorie:325 kPa. This is approximately 4.190 J. 6. International Steam Table Calorie (1929): Defined as (1/860) watt-hours or (180/43) joules, which is approximately 4.1868 J. 7. International Steam Table Calorie (1956) (calIT): Defined as 1.163 milliwatt-hours, or exactly 4.1868 J. This definition was adopted during the Fifth International Conference on Properties of Steam in London in July 1956. 8. IUNS calorie: Defined as exactly 4.182 J. This definition was adopted by the Committee on Nomenclature of the International Union of Nutritional Sciences. Among these definitions, the 15°C calorie and the thermochemical calorie were historically the most widely used in older scientific literature. However, the existence of multiple definitions has caused significant confusion and errors. Consequently, the use of all calorie definitions has been deprecated in favor of the joule (J), the SI unit for heat and energy.
